Are we focusing on the wrong cost in the heat pump transition?

A lot of the conversation around heat pump adoption has focused on one challenge: making them more affordable to install.

And rightly so.

But installation is only the beginning.

The homeowner then has to live with the system.

That means the economics of the heat transition need to work in three places:

1. Acquisition — what does it cost to install?
2. Operation — what does it cost to live with?
3. Performance — has the system been designed well enough to deliver what is expected of it?

With electricity and gas prices continuing to shape the running-cost conversation, we think this distinction is becoming increasingly important.

Our latest article looks at why the next phase of heat pump adoption needs to focus not only on how many systems we install, but on how many we make work exceptionally well.

What do you think is the biggest economic barrier to wider heat pump adoption today?

The first cold snap is the real inspection for every heat pump installed this year.

In the October edition of Energy in the Field: heat pumps now outship gas furnaces, a bad install can quietly cost a customer about 30 percent, and five moves programs can make before the first hard freeze.

Program managers, weatherization directors and installers: when a heat pump underperforms in its first winter, who finds out first? Tell me in the comments.

One of the biggest challenges facing the heat-pump industry is that customers naturally compare new technology with the heating experience they already know.

For decades, homeowners have associated good heating with very hot radiators and rapid bursts of heat. Heat pumps are designed around a different objective: maintaining a consistently comfortable home while using energy more efficiently.
That distinction matters commercially.

If the industry continues to sell heat pumps simply as replacements for boilers, without properly explaining how the experience differs, we risk creating uncertainty and setting the wrong expectations.

Successful heat-pump adoption requires more than good technology. It requires accurate system design, high-quality installation and a clear customer journey that helps homeowners understand what good performance should actually feel like.

Ultimately, customers don’t buy hot radiators or technical specifications. They buy comfort, confidence and predictable running costs.

That is the proposition our industry needs to communicate more effectively.
#HeatPumps #HomeComfort #CustomerExperience #LowCarbonHeating #RenewableEnergy

In my 36 years in this industry, the barriers to adoption in the UK have been design quality, installation standards, upfront cost and an electricity price that is still set by gas. A new working fluid does not address any of these. I will follow the BlueHeart and Ecoforest work with interest, and I would like to see measured seasonal performance at 55°C flow when the first units reach the market in 2027.

I welcome the work that Adrián describes here, and I would like to see thermoacoustic and caloric heat pumps succeed. There are some questions that I think the industry should ask before it treats them as the next revolution.

With R290, the climate case against refrigerants has largely been answered, as its GWP is in low single figures. The issue that remains is flammability, which affects charge limits and where a unit can be installed. Removing that would be a real benefit, particularly for packaged ground source units in plant rooms, but it must not come at the cost of efficiency.

Neither article gives a COP. Vapour compression is difficult to beat because it uses latent heat, and a refrigerant-free machine that runs at a lower seasonal efficiency than a good R290 unit would add more emissions through electricity use than it saves in refrigerant risk.

The elastocaloric result of 400 W across a 41 K span is a good laboratory figure, but space heating requires several kilowatts at a similar or greater lift under load. The million-cycle durability figure also depends on frequency, and a domestic heat pump needs to run for around 20 years.

Thermoacoustic machines are being presented as a solution for homes that need high flow temperatures. I would rather that we designed those homes to run at lower flow temperatures, which every heat pump can already do well.
